power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

:::

table.title: Do Social-Emotional Teaching Skills Increase with Teaching Experience in Brazil?
table.existing_data_explanation: It's complicated. We have already collected some data but explain in Question 8 why readers may consider this a valid pre-registration nevertheless.
table.research_questions: In this survey study, we are examining 19 social-emotional teaching (SET) skills and test whether the 19 SET scales can be predicted from three "independent variables": teaching experience, age, and gender. We hypothesized that a subset of these SET skills would increase with teaching experience, but to fully understand these effects, the teacher's age has to be taken into consideration as well. Moreover, we expected that female and male teachers would differ on a subset of these SET skills. See Section 5 (Analyses) for details on the seven SET skills this research will focus on. To test these hypotheses, we used an unusually large sample of more than 43,000 teachers in the state of São Paulo, Brazil. We divided this sample randomly into two halves, the Derivation sample (DS) and the Replication sample (RS). We have used the Derivation sample to conduct an initial set of correlation and regression analyses. The goal of this preregistration is to describe our procedures and hypothesis tests that we now plan to conduct in the Replication sample. Our hypotheses are described below in Section 5 (Analyses) and are based on the findings of the exploratory analyses in the Derivation sample.
table.design_dependent_variables: Here we are studying 19 scales measuring social-emotional teaching (SET) skills. These scales have five items on average and the mean of the alpha reliability coefficients was .68 in the Derivation sample.
table.study_design_overview: This is a cross-sectional survey study, so there are no conditions. However, we will test whether the 19 SET scales can be predicted from three "independent variables": teaching experience, age, and gender.
table.statistical_tests:
We will replicate the regression analyses from the Derivation sample. In these regressions, we enter teaching experience, the quadratic effect of teaching experience (to test whether gains in SET skills happen early during the teaching career or slow towards the end of the teaching career), age (to control for the inherent correlation between teaching experience and age, which was .65 in the Derivation sample), and gender. We also ran analyses including the interaction between teaching experience and gender to test whether the impact of teaching experience might be different for women than for men. However, these interaction effects were all small and only one (Connection and Caring) exceeded (a) an effect size of beta = .025 and (b) a conservative p level of .001 in this very large sample. We will replicate these regressions exactly as we ran them in the Derivation sample and also check whether the interactions between teaching experience and gender are again small. For this preregistration, we focus on seven of our 19 SET variables that show theoretically meaningful and interesting patterns of the interplay between teaching experience, age, and gender, which are briefly summarized below. 
(a) We expected that Communication and Presentation skills would show an increase with teaching experience, especially early in the teaching career, implying both a positive linear effect of teaching experience and a negative quadratic effect. This was indeed the case, with the relevant betas being .134 and -.036, respectively. Age did not have an effect (beta = -.002), and men scored higher than women (beta = .112). 
(b) For Managing Classroom Behavior, we again found a positive linear effect (beta = .101) and a negative quadratic effect (beta = -.029). Here the age effect went in the same direction as the teaching experience effect (beta = .045), indicating that both greater teaching experience and being an older teacher make it easier to manage difficult student behavior in the classroom. Women and men did not differ. 
(c) For Connection and Caring, we found only a linear effect of teaching experience and the age effect went in the same direction, both relatively small effects; as expected, women scored higher than men. Here we found the only reasonably sized interaction of teaching experience and gender, with a beta of .028 (p < .001), indicating that the effect of teaching experience was stronger for women than for men. 
(d) For Passion for Learning and Understanding, we had not expected any strong effects. The betas indicated a small positive effect of teaching experience, and that men scored somewhat higher than women. 
**See Question 8 for continuation.
table.outliers_and_exclusions: A total of 49,020 teachers completed the survey. In this initial set, 2,172 were duplicate responses, so only the first assessment of each participant was kept in the database, resulting in 46,848 participants. In a second step, we examined the four attention-check control items: 85.4% of the participants answered all attention-check items correctly; 8.4% failed one, 2.8% failed two, 2.7% failed three, and 0.5% failed four. Participants that failed two or more attention checks were filtered out (N = 3,021). Finally, 809 were deleted because they made a mistake entering their age (i.e., they indicated they were below 18 or above 80 years old), resulting in a final data set of 43,018. That is, our sample includes 22.4% of the total number of teachers employed by the state of São Paulo at the time. One-half of the total sample was randomly assigned to the Derivation sample (N = 21,509). In this sample, 73% were women, very similar to the 72% who were women in the overall population of teachers in the state. The average participant was 45 years old (SD = 10 years), with a range from 20 to 75. The age distribution in the sample was as follows: 490 were between 20-25 years old; 1,132 were 25-30 years; 1,977 were 30-35 years; 2,932 were 35-40 years; 3,494 were 40-45 years; 3,743 were 45-50 years; 3,279 were 50-55 years; 2,200 were 55-60 years, 935 were 60-65 years and 291 were over 65 years old. Because teachers typically retire by 65 or earlier, we omitted the very small group of teachers beyond retirement age for all the analyses. We did this because here we aim to evaluate tenure effects, controlling for age, and thus needed a coherent end-point for the age variable. In addition, we found that some teachers made a mistake in recording either their age or their tenure (i.e., their reported tenure was implausible given their reported age); these teachers were also excluded from the analyses in the Derivation sample. We plan to make these two data exclusions in the Replication sample as well. We also evaluated how representative our sample is of the full population of teachers in terms of age. The education department at the state of Sao Paulo provided us with age statistics for ten-year age ranges of all teachers in the public education system, allowing us to compute the representation of each ten-year age group from 20 to 60 years in the Derivation sample. As expected, the youngest group from 20-29 years (which is the most technology savvy and open to surveys), showed the highest participation rate (28%). The three older age groups participated in roughly the same percentages with 22% for age 30-39, 21% for age 40-49, and 19% for age 50-59. In other words, the age distribution in the Derivation sample was similar to the entire population with a slight oversampling of teachers in their twenties.
table.sample_size:
No need to justify decision, but be precise about exactly how the number will be determined.
The final data set included 43,018 public school teachers (that is, 22.4% of the total number of teachers employed by the state of São Paulo at the time). These teacher data were obtained through the education department in São Paulo state, Brazil. The education department invited all 196,000 teachers teaching in the Middle school or High school in the public education system to participate in the study using e-mails, intranet communications, and messages on other channels. The message included a direct link to access the assessment platform, where teachers could enter using their employee ID information. The teachers eligible for participation were pre-registered on the platform to limit access. In other words, participation was limited to teachers who were currently teaching in grades 6-12. To allow for exploratory and confirmatory purposes of this study, the dataset was randomly split into two subsamples. Each dataset had N = 21,509 participants. In the Derivation sample (where the teachers in retirement age were excluded), mean age was 45.4 years (SD = 9.72).
table.additional_comments:
Why should this still be considered a valid preregistration? Although the data collection is already finished, we did not analyze the data from the Replication sample. The present preregistration is meant to explicitly outline our methods and expectations on how teaching experience (i.e., number of years teaching) predicts teacher social-emotional skills in a new sample that provides a direct replication of the findings from Derivation sample. 
** Continuation Question 5: 
(e) For Collaborating with Parents, we found a positive linear effect of teaching experience and a strong age effect, indicating that both older and more experienced teachers have better skills in dealing with parents. As expected, women were somewhat more skilled in dealing with parents. 
(f) For Mindsets about Students' Learning, we found a negative effect of age, indicating that older teachers did not have as strong beliefs about the inherent growth potential of all students as the younger teachers did (beta = -.106) whereas teaching experience was essentially irrelevant (beta = .018). 
(g) Finally, the results for Stress Resilience and Recovery showed the most complex pattern, where we had expected a negative effect of teaching experience (i.e., length of employment). This was indeed the case: the beta was -.136 for the linear effect (indicating a decrease) and .086 for the quadratic effect (indicating a slowing of the decrease). These effects were interestingly complicated by the positive effect of age. Specifically, teaching experience led to a decrease in Stress Resilience and Recovery when each of the major age groups in the sample was considered separately (i.e., teachers in their 20s, 30s, 40s, 50s, and the smaller group from 60-65). In addition, these five age groups showed a linear increase, with older teachers showing greater Stress Resilience and Recovery. Men scored slightly higher than women. 
In addition, we will report these regression analyses for the 12 remaining scales and also illustrate these effects in graphs that show the effect of teaching experience separately for the five age groups (see above) and for men and women. Moreover, to provide basic effects information, we also report the simple correlations between the four predictors (teaching experience, teaching experience squared, age, and gender).

text.text: Background: Teachers and students share the same classroom, but they may perceive teacher behavior differently.
Understanding these perceptual differences is important because students' experiences of teaching may be linked to their well-being.

Aims: This study examined teacher-student agreement on teachers' social-emotional and instructional characteristics, tested whether student-rated characteristics were associated with student well-being, and investigated whether teacher-student alignment predicted well-being beyond either perspective alone.
Participants were 1,994 students and 143 secondary school teachers from Belgium.

Methods: Teachers and students completed parallel ratings of 35 classroom-relevant teacher behaviors using a Too Little/Too Much response format, indicating whether behaviors were perceived as insufficient, optimal, or excessive.

Analyses included teacher-student agreement correlations, multilevel models testing linear and quadratic associations with student wellbeing, and response surface analyses examining teacher-student alignment.
Results: Teacher-student agreement was modest overall, with an average correlation of r = .18.
Teachers generally rated their behavior as closer to the optimal level than students did.

Several student-rated characteristics showed curvilinear associations with well-being, including teaching pace, openness to different opinions, patience, and emotional self-control, indicating that both perceived deficits and excesses were associated with lower well-being.

Teacher-student misalignment predicted lower student well-being beyond teacher and student ratings considered separately for several characteristics, including support for mentally struggling students and instructional pacing.
Conclusions: Students provide a distinct and consequential perspective on teaching.
Effective teaching may depend not only on whether desirable behaviors are present, but also on whether they are perceived as appropriately calibrated.
Teachers and students share the same classroom yet often experience it through different lenses (Elen & Lowyck, 1998).
text.formatted: Teachers and students share the same classroom yet often experience it through different lenses <ref type="bibr" target="#b8">(Elen & Lowyck, 1998)</ref>.

text.text: This matters because key classroom processes -how instruction is structured, how disruptions are handled, how supportive the learning climate feels -are not only defined by what teachers do, but by how students perceive those behaviors.

In this study, we focus on teachers' social-emotional and instructional (SEI) characteristics: a broad set of teacher behaviors spanning relational support, emotion regulation, instructional communication, classroom management, and innovative teaching practices (Scheirlinckx et al., 2026).
text.formatted: In this study, we focus on teachers' social-emotional and instructional (SEI) characteristics: a broad set of teacher behaviors spanning relational support, emotion regulation, instructional communication, classroom management, and innovative teaching practices <ref type="bibr">(Scheirlinckx et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: These characteristics are foundational to classroom functioning.

According to the prosocial classroom model (Jennings & Greenberg, 2009), teachers' social and emotional competence underlies their capacity to build supportive relationships, manage classroom dynamics effectively, and foster a climate conducive to students' academic and emotional development.
text.formatted: According to the prosocial classroom model <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">(Jennings & Greenberg, 2009)</ref>, teachers' social and emotional competence underlies their capacity to build supportive relationships, manage classroom dynamics effectively, and foster a climate conducive to students' academic and emotional development.

text.text: SEI characteristics thus represent the behavioral mechanisms through which teachers shape not only how much students learn, but how students experience school.

Despite the relevance of teachers' SEI characteristics, many studies rely on a single informant, often the teacher, to report on instructional practices and social-emotional attributes (Lauermann & Hagen 2021).
text.formatted: Despite the relevance of teachers' SEI characteristics, many studies rely on a single informant, often the teacher, to report on instructional practices and social-emotional attributes <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">(Lauermann & Hagen 2021)</ref>.

text.text: However, evidence consistently suggests that students and teachers often disagree in their perceptions of what happens in the classroom, particularly regarding classroom management and emotional support (den Brok et al., 2006; Scherzinger & Wettstein, 2018).
text.formatted: However, evidence consistently suggests that students and teachers often disagree in their perceptions of what happens in the classroom, particularly regarding classroom management and emotional support (den <ref type="bibr" target="#b5">Brok et al., 2006;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Scherzinger & Wettstein, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Importantly, these discrepancies are not trivial-external observers often align more closely with students' perceptions than with teachers' self-reports (De Jong & Westerhof, 2001; Scherzinger & Wettstein, 2018), suggesting that student reports capture meaningful variation in classroom processes that may be underestimated when relying solely on teachers' perspectives.
text.formatted: Importantly, these discrepancies are not trivial-external observers often align more closely with students' perceptions than with teachers' self-reports <ref type="bibr" target="#b6">(De Jong & Westerhof, 2001;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">Scherzinger & Wettstein, 2018)</ref>, suggesting that student reports capture meaningful variation in classroom processes that may be underestimated when relying solely on teachers' perspectives.

text.text: Building on this multi-perspective view, the present study assesses teachers' SEI characteristics using both teacher self-ratings and student ratings of the same teacher behaviors.
Methodologically, combining perspectives from both informants reduces sharedmethod bias and strengthens construct validity (Kankaraš & Suarez-Alvarez, 2019).
text.formatted: Methodologically, combining perspectives from both informants reduces sharedmethod bias and strengthens construct validity <ref type="bibr" target="#b19">(Kankaraš & Suarez-Alvarez, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Substantively, it allows us to test whether student-rated SEI characteristics are predictive of student outcomes and what agreement between teachers and students means for students' well-being.
Teachers are widely recognized as the most influential in-school factor in shaping students' academic achievement and well-being (Hanushek & Rivkin, 2010; López-Martín et al., 2023).
text.formatted: Teachers are widely recognized as the most influential in-school factor in shaping students' academic achievement and well-being <ref type="bibr" target="#b16">(Hanushek & Rivkin, 2010;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b25">López-Martín et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: They do far more than deliver course content.
They model behavior, regulate classroom climate, and form relationships that significantly affect students' development (Blazar & Kraft, 2017; Emilia et al., 2023).
text.formatted: They model behavior, regulate classroom climate, and form relationships that significantly affect students' development <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Blazar & Kraft, 2017;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b9">Emilia et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: Accordingly, teaching quality is increasingly conceptualized as a combination of a) instructional competencies (e.g., providing structure, clarity, cognitively challenging learning opportunities) and b) social-emotional competencies (e.g., emotion regulation, perspective-taking, classroom management, adaptive and innovative practices; Klusmann et al., 2022).
text.formatted: Accordingly, teaching quality is increasingly conceptualized as a combination of a) instructional competencies (e.g., providing structure, clarity, cognitively challenging learning opportunities) and b) social-emotional competencies (e.g., emotion regulation, perspective-taking, classroom management, adaptive and innovative practices; <ref type="bibr" target="#b22">Klusmann et al., 2022)</ref>.

text.text: In this paper, we refer to this broader set of teacher and teaching qualities as teacher social-emotional and instructional (SEI) characteristics.

This integrated view aligns with the prosocial classroom model by Jennings and Greenberg (2009), which posits that teachers' social and emotional competence is foundational for building supportive teacher-student relationships and effective classroom management.
text.formatted: This integrated view aligns with the prosocial classroom model by <ref type="bibr" target="#b18">Jennings and Greenberg (2009)</ref>, which posits that teachers' social and emotional competence is foundational for building supportive teacher-student relationships and effective classroom management.

text.text: These capacities, in turn, foster a classroom climate conducive to students' academic and emotional functioning.

SEI characteristics matter precisely because they shape day-to-day classroom interactions and learning opportunities, with consequences for students' longer-term academic and emotional development (e.g., Zins et al., 2007).
text.formatted: SEI characteristics matter precisely because they shape day-to-day classroom interactions and learning opportunities, with consequences for students' longer-term academic and emotional development (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b47">Zins et al., 2007)</ref>.

text.text: For example, teachers' emotion regulation is associated with more effective management of disruptions and higher student engagement (Rimm-Kaufman & Hamre, 2010), and positive teacher-student relationships are associated with greater school engagement and fewer behavioral problems (Marzano & Marzano, 2003; Pianta et al., 2003; Quin, 2017).
text.formatted: For example, teachers' emotion regulation is associated with more effective management of disruptions and higher student engagement <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">(Rimm-Kaufman & Hamre, 2010)</ref>, and positive teacher-student relationships are associated with greater school engagement and fewer behavioral problems <ref type="bibr" target="#b26">(Marzano & Marzano, 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b30">Pianta et al., 2003;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b32">Quin, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: Metaanalytic evidence also indicates that classroom management interventions or strategies show small but reliable associations with students' academic, behavioral, and social-emotional outcomes (Korpershoek et al., 2016).
text.formatted: Metaanalytic evidence also indicates that classroom management interventions or strategies show small but reliable associations with students' academic, behavioral, and social-emotional outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b13">(Korpershoek et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: Complementing this work, research suggests that teachers influence both students' cognitive skills and their social-emotional development (Kraft, 2019).
text.formatted: Complementing this work, research suggests that teachers influence both students' cognitive skills and their social-emotional development <ref type="bibr" target="#b23">(Kraft, 2019)</ref>.

text.text: Taken together, these findings position SEI characteristics as plausible mechanisms through which teachers shape not only how much students learn, but also how students experience school.
At the same time, evidence is not uniformly strong nor linear across SEI domains and outcomes.

Some associations appear to operate through intermediate classroom processes (e.g., classroom climate, management, or support), and effects can vary depending on measurement source, operationalization, and context (e.g., Fauth et al., 2019).
text.formatted: Some associations appear to operate through intermediate classroom processes (e.g., classroom climate, management, or support), and effects can vary depending on measurement source, operationalization, and context (e.g., <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">Fauth et al., 2019)</ref>.

text.text: This motivates a more finegrained approach that (a) differentiates among SEI characteristics, (b) incorporates multiple perspectives, and (c) allows for nonlinear assessment of teachers' competencies.

Student ratings are sometimes criticized as weak proxies for "true" teaching effectiveness or learning outcomes, particularly when effectiveness is defined narrowly in terms of grade-based achievement (Van der Lans & Maulana, 2018).
text.formatted: Student ratings are sometimes criticized as weak proxies for "true" teaching effectiveness or learning outcomes, particularly when effectiveness is defined narrowly in terms of grade-based achievement <ref type="bibr" target="#b42">(Van der Lans & Maulana, 2018)</ref>.

text.text: However, students are also closerange observers of teachers' day-to-day behavior, especially instructional, relational, and emotional practices that are most salient during lessons.

Research suggests that students are sensitive to teachers' interpersonal behaviors (e.g., empathy, communication), and these perceptions can shape how students experience the classroom (Ryan & Patrick, 2001).
text.formatted: Research suggests that students are sensitive to teachers' interpersonal behaviors (e.g., empathy, communication), and these perceptions can shape how students experience the classroom <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Ryan & Patrick, 2001)</ref>.

text.text: In line with this, research on classroom environments indicates that students' perceptions of psychosocial classroom characteristics shape students' well-being.

For example, in Belgian secondary education, students reported higher well-being when they perceived their teacher's interpersonal behavior as tolerant instead of authoritarian (Van Petegem et al., 2007 , 2008).
text.formatted: For example, in Belgian secondary education, students reported higher well-being when they perceived their teacher's interpersonal behavior as tolerant instead of authoritarian <ref type="bibr" target="#b43">(Van Petegem et al., 2007</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">, 2008)</ref>.

text.text: In other words, student ratings may not merely reflect bias, but rather a substantively important perspective on classroom processes, especially for SEI characteristics.
This is consistent with evidence that students' perceptions of classroom interactions are systematically related to their engagement in school.
In a multilevel study of Norwegian students, perceived emotional support of teachers was associated with higher emotional and behavioral engagement of students (Havik & Westergård, 2020).
text.formatted: In a multilevel study of Norwegian students, perceived emotional support of teachers was associated with higher emotional and behavioral engagement of students <ref type="bibr" target="#b17">(Havik & Westergård, 2020)</ref>.

text.text: Alternatively, Collie (2021) found that teachers' instructional support was not directly related to students' emotional well-being outcomes but indirectly related via students' perceived competence.
text.formatted: Alternatively, <ref type="bibr" target="#b4">Collie (2021)</ref> found that teachers' instructional support was not directly related to students' emotional well-being outcomes but indirectly related via students' perceived competence.

text.text: Student reports are especially informative when teaching behaviors have an "optimal zone" because students can indicate not only whether a behavior is present, but whether it feels insufficient, appropriate, or excessive.

For some teaching behaviors, both insufficient and overly excessive levels may be associated with poorer outcomes, implying curvilinear (optimality) relationships rather than strictly linear ones (Vergauwe et al., 2017).
text.formatted: For some teaching behaviors, both insufficient and overly excessive levels may be associated with poorer outcomes, implying curvilinear (optimality) relationships rather than strictly linear ones <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Vergauwe et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: For instance, caring for students is typically beneficial, but when support becomes overly intense or intrusive (e.g., crossing boundaries, monitoring), it can undermine students' autonomy and relate to less adaptive functioning.
A similar pattern may apply to teacher humor.

A study found that moderate use of humor increased student enjoyment and reduced boredom, yet excessive humor unrelated to the course content was perceived as distracting and was linked to lower enjoyment and higher boredom (Bieg et al., 2017).
text.formatted: A study found that moderate use of humor increased student enjoyment and reduced boredom, yet excessive humor unrelated to the course content was perceived as distracting and was linked to lower enjoyment and higher boredom <ref type="bibr" target="#b1">(Bieg et al., 2017)</ref>.

text.text: They also found that, when taken too far, aggressive humor and sarcasm (e.g., when the teacher makes fun of the students) were associated with lower enjoyment and heightened anxiety.

Evidence for such nonlinear patterns also exists in the instructional domain: inquirybased teaching (i.e., a student-centered teaching approach that reverses traditional instruction by starting with questions and problems, rather than presenting facts) has been shown to be related to student achievement in a curvilinear way, with moderate levels sometimes being most beneficial (Teig et al., 2018).
text.formatted: Evidence for such nonlinear patterns also exists in the instructional domain: inquirybased teaching (i.e., a student-centered teaching approach that reverses traditional instruction by starting with questions and problems, rather than presenting facts) has been shown to be related to student achievement in a curvilinear way, with moderate levels sometimes being most beneficial <ref type="bibr">(Teig et al., 2018)</ref>.

text.text: Capturing these patterns requires measures that can capture deviations in both directions.
Many studies assess teaching characteristics using traditional Likert-type agreement scales (e.g., from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree").
Although widely used, this format has well-known limitations when the construct of interest is optimality rather than amount.

This limitation is especially relevant for SEI characteristics, which may follow a "too much of a good thing" logic: beyond some point, additional increases can become unhelpful or even counterproductive (Pierce & Aguinis, 2013).
text.formatted: This limitation is especially relevant for SEI characteristics, which may follow a "too much of a good thing" logic: beyond some point, additional increases can become unhelpful or even counterproductive <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Pierce & Aguinis, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Likert responses are shaped by a process in which respondents interpret an item relative to their own frame of reference (Ogden & Lo, 2012).
text.formatted: Likert responses are shaped by a process in which respondents interpret an item relative to their own frame of reference <ref type="bibr" target="#b28">(Ogden & Lo, 2012)</ref>.

text.text: As a result, Likert ratings often obscure qualitatively different perceptions.

For example, disagreeing with the item "The teacher provides sufficient structure" does not reveal whether students experience too little structure (chaotic, unclear) or too much structure (rigid, controlling).
This ambiguity becomes especially problematic for SEI behaviors where both deficits and excesses can have consequences for students.
A second limitation is that Likert scales can be relatively insensitive at the extremes.

When response options run from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree," it is often unclear what the endpoints actually represent in practice, especially for behaviors that vary in frequency or intensity (Schwartz et al., 1991).
text.formatted: When response options run from "strongly disagree" to "strongly agree," it is often unclear what the endpoints actually represent in practice, especially for behaviors that vary in frequency or intensity <ref type="bibr">(Schwartz et al., 1991)</ref>.

text.text: For example, two students might both select "strongly agree" to "The teacher is involved in students' personal lives", with one student experiencing the teacher as supportive without crossing boundaries, whereas the other experiences the same teacher as overly involved; the classic Likert-scale does not allow to distinguish "high involvement but still appropriate" from "too much involvement".
Conversely, two students could choose different options (e.g., "agree" vs. "strongly agree") while still sharing the same underlying judgment that the teacher shows the right amount of involvement.

To address these issues, we use the Too Little/Too Much (TLTM) response format, introduced in leadership research and recently used in personality research to capture deviations from an ideal level (Dupré et al., 2022; Kaplan & Kaiser, 2006).
text.formatted: To address these issues, we use the Too Little/Too Much (TLTM) response format, introduced in leadership research and recently used in personality research to capture deviations from an ideal level <ref type="bibr" target="#b7">(Dupré et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">Kaplan & Kaiser, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: TLTM frames each behavior on a bidirectional continuum anchored around "the right amount", typically ranging from "much too little", "about right" to "much too much."
This design allows for clearer interpretation of responses: a rating communicates not only whether a behavior is present, but whether it is perceived as insufficient, optimal, or excessive.

TLTM is particularly valuable for SEI characteristics because many teaching behaviors likely follow an optimality ("more is not always better") logic: too little enthusiasm can feel disengaged, whereas too much can feel overwhelming.

Importantly, evidence for the added value of TLTM comes primarily from leadership and individual-differences research, where "too little/too much" formats have been shown to capture curvilinear associations and improve interpretability compared with unidirectional Likert ratings (Kaplan & Kaiser, 2006).
text.formatted: Importantly, evidence for the added value of TLTM comes primarily from leadership and individual-differences research, where "too little/too much" formats have been shown to capture curvilinear associations and improve interpretability compared with unidirectional Likert ratings <ref type="bibr" target="#b20">(Kaplan & Kaiser, 2006)</ref>.

text.text: Building on this methodological work, we apply TLTM to teaching-specific SEI behaviors to test whether similar optimality patterns emerge in classroom settings.
Overall, TLTM measurement aligns with the idea that effective teaching involves calibration and balance rather than simple maximization of teaching characteristics.
Importantly, however, the "right amount" is not necessarily the same for every student.

Students differ in their needs for structure, autonomy, emotional closeness, and stimulation, meaning that a behavior experienced as supportive by one student may feel intrusive, rigid, or overwhelming to another.
This is a further reason to rely on student ratings and to use TLTM specifically.
TLTM does not assume one normative "best" level of a behavior; instead, it records whether each student experiences the teacher's behavior as insufficient, appropriate, or excessive.

Most work on teaching effectiveness targets a narrow slice of classroom functioning (e.g., classroom management or emotion regulation) and often relies on a single informant to capture this information (Schulz et al., 2014).
text.formatted: Most work on teaching effectiveness targets a narrow slice of classroom functioning (e.g., classroom management or emotion regulation) and often relies on a single informant to capture this information <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Schulz et al., 2014)</ref>.

text.text: Building on calls for broader, multi-perspective assessments, the present study examines teachers' SEI characteristics using (a) a comprehensive taxonomy of classroom-relevant teacher behaviors, (b) parallel teacher self-ratings and student ratings of the same characteristics, and (c) a TLTM response format that captures perceived deviations from an optimal level.
This design allows us to move beyond the question of whether SEI characteristics matter, and to address how they are perceived (and whether those perceptions converge) in everyday classroom life.
First, we assess teacher-student agreement across a broad set of teachers' SEI characteristics, quantifying overall alignment and identifying systematic gaps between self-and student perceptions.

Second, we examine whether student-rated SEI characteristics relate to student well-being and academic performance, because students' reports may capture classroom-relevant variation not fully reflected in teachers' self-reports.

Third, we test whether alignment versus misalignment in SEI ratings predicts well-being and performance beyond teacher and student ratings considered separately, including whether outcomes are strongest when both perspectives converge at optimal levels and whether specific discrepancy patterns (e.g., teachers rating themselves more optimally than students, or vice versa) are linked to poorer outcomes.

Across these aims, we assess a broad set of SEI characteristics spanning bonding and connecting characteristics (e.g., connecting and caring, empathic awareness, trusting students, responsiveness to diversity, growth mindset), instruction and communication (e.g., clarity, humor, pacing), organization (e.g., planning, student engagement management), and innovative practice (e.g., flexibility, creative teaching, reflective practice, appreciating diversity), alongside teachers' emotional self-regulation and stress resilience.

By integrating dual perspectives with a comprehensive set of SEI characteristics, this study contributes to a more fine-grained and ecologically grounded understanding of how teacher SEI characteristics relate to student outcomes.
A total of 143 secondary education teachers from 41 schools participated, each rating one class with which they had the most weekly contact, resulting in 143 unique teacher-class combinations.
Their mean age was 42.15 years (SD = 10.82, range: 23-63).
The gender distribution closely reflected the broader Flemish teaching workforce, with 65% identifying as women (Flemish Ministry of Education and Training, 2023).
On average, teachers had 17.83 years of teaching experience (SD = 10.36) and taught 19 hours per week (SD = 4).
A total of 2,031 students completed the questionnaire.
After excluding cases with missing key variables or indications of poor data quality (e.g., identical responses across all items; Gosling et al., 2004), the final sample consisted of 1,994 students.

Students' mean age was 15.41 years (SD = 1.93, range: 11-20), spanning all six years of Flemish secondary education.

The broad age range reflects the full scope of the secondary school system and is acknowledged as a source of heterogeneity; student age was included as a covariate in all analyses to partially account for this variation.
Teachers were recruited via university student networks and professional contacts across Flanders.

Teachers from special education and those teaching the participating class exclusively in physical education were excluded, as the distinct educational context of these settings would affect the interpretability of SEI ratings.

All exclusion criteria, research hypotheses, and primary analysis plans were preregistered on AsPredicted before data collection; analyses not specified in the preregistration are treated as exploratory and are identified as such in the results.
Each participating teacher selected one class for inclusion.

Students in these classes completed a short questionnaire (approximately 10 minutes) rating their teacher's SEI characteristics and reporting on their own well-being and academic performance, either on paper or online.
Teachers completed a separate online survey (approximately 40 minutes) assessing their own SEI characteristics and demographic information.
Teacher and student data collection occurred within the same one-week period per class to minimize temporal mismatch between perspectives.
Written informed consent was obtained from all teachers and students; parental consent was additionally obtained for students under 18.
The study was approved by the institutional ethics committee.

Teachers and students completed parallel versions of the same items: teachers provided selfratings of their own classroom behavior, and students rated the same behaviors for their teacher.

Both versions used the Too Little/Too Much (TLTM) response format (Kaplan & Kaiser, 2006), in which respondents indicate whether the teacher showed much too little (-2), too little (-1), the right amount (0), too much (+1), or much too much (+2) of each behavior.

This format is explicitly designed to capture deviations from an optimal level in both directions, making it well-suited for detecting curvilinear associations in which both deficits and excesses may relate to poorer outcomes.
Items were phrased positively and descriptively, avoiding evaluative language, as the TLTM scale itself conveys evaluation.

Student well-being was assessed using the Student Subjective Well-being Questionnaire (SSWQ; Renshaw, 2020), a 16-item scale covering four dimensions: Joy of Learning, School Connectedness, Educational Purpose, and Academic Efficacy.
Items are rated on a four-point Likert scale ranging from 1 (almost never) to 4 (almost always).
Following prior applications of this instrument, scores were aggregated into a single composite well-being score.

Internal consistencies were good, with McDonald's omega for the total well-being scale being ω = .85, ω = .76 for Joy of Learning; ω =.77 for School Connectedness; ω = .74 for Educational Purpose; and ω = .87 for Academic Efficacy.
Because students were nested within teachers, all analyses used two-level hierarchical linear models with students at Level 1 and teachers at Level 2.

To evaluate whether a third school level was warranted, we estimated unconditional three-level models; likelihood ratio tests indicated that the school level did not significantly improve model fit (p = .15), and all subsequent analyses used two-level models.
To evaluate within-class consistency of student ratings and justify the use of aggregated student scores in RQ1 and RQ3, we computed ICC1 and ICC2 values for all 35 SEI items.
ICC1 values ranged from .04 to .31 (M = .14), indicating that on average 14% of the variance in student ratings was attributable to the teacher level.
ICC2 values ranged from .35 to .86 (M = .66), supporting the reliability of class-mean aggregates for use in subsequent analyses.

text.text: Agreement was strongest for observable instructional behaviors -using personal anecdotes in class (ρ = .41) and following a lesson plan (ρ = .36) -whereas items reflecting internal beliefs or less visible relational processes showed near-zero associations, such as believing that every student can learn (ρ = .00) and being open to different opinions (ρ = .09).
This pattern is consistent with the interpersonal perception model (Kenny, 1994), whereby behaviorally salient behaviors yield higher agreement than beliefs or intentions.
Beyond rank-order agreement, teachers generally perceived their own behavior as closer to the optimal level than their students did.
The largest gaps appeared for adapting when a lesson goes differently than expected (dz = -.53), starting the lesson optimistically (dz = -.50), and using humor in class (dz = -.48).

For a smaller set of items, students rated teachers as more optimal than teachers rated themselves, most notably for wanting to improve oneself as a teacher (dz = .39) and addressing diversity issues (dz = .38).
Together, these findings suggest that teacher self-reports and student perceptions are complementary rather than interchangeable sources of information.

In practical terms, these effects suggest that both extremes of these behaviors are associated with lower student well-being.

For example, well-being was lower when students perceived teachers as providing too little active engagement, increased as engagement approached an optimal level, but declined again at very high levels -suggesting that overly intensive engagement can feel intrusive or exhausting.

Similarly, well-being was lowest when instructional pace was perceived as either too slow or too fast, and highest around a moderate level that supports comprehension without inducing boredom or overload.

A smaller set of positive linear effects also emerged -trusting students, controlling negative emotions, and experimenting with new teaching methods -though for several of these, a significant negative quadratic term indicated diminishing returns at higher levels.

Teaching pace additionally showed a negative linear component alongside its quadratic effect, suggesting directional asymmetry: being perceived as too fast was more detrimental to wellbeing than being perceived as too slow.

This aligns with cognitive load accounts of instruction, whereby rapid presentation overwhelms working memory and impairs encoding (Sweller, 2011), and with evidence that time-compressed speech degrades comprehension once input rates exceed processing limits (Peelle & Davis, 2012).

To test whether teacher-student (mis)alignment predicts student well-being beyond either perspective alone, we compared baseline polynomial models including teacher ratings, class-mean student ratings, and their squared terms against alignment models additionally including the teacher × student mean interaction term.

Significant interaction effects were interpreted using response surface analysis (RSA) parameters for the line of congruence (LOC; a1: slope, a2: curvature) and line of incongruence (LOIC; a3: directional asymmetry, a4: mismatch penalty).

Adding the interaction term significantly improved model fit for seven SEI items: supporting students who are mentally struggling, being open to different opinions, actively engaging students, distancing oneself from stressful situations, having patience, speaking pace, and teaching pace (full RSA parameters reported in Supplementary Materials Table S5).

text.text: Across all seven significant effects, the curvature of the line of incongruence (a4) was consistently negative (range: -.19 to -.69), indicating a mismatch penalty: student well-being was highest when teacher and student ratings were similar and decreased as discrepancies grew in either direction.

The slope of the line of incongruence (a3) was consistently small (range: -.11 to .01), suggesting little directional asymmetry -the well-being cost of disagreement did not differ substantially depending on whether teachers rated themselves more optimally than students or vice versa.
In other words, the magnitude of the mismatch mattered more than its direction.

Do teachers and students experience the classroom in the same way?
Does student well-being improve when students rate their teacher more favorably?
And does alignment between teacher and student perspectives matter beyond either perspective alone?
The present study examined these questions by assessing teachers' social-emotional and instructional (SEI) characteristics from dual perspectives and linking these perceptions to student wellbeing.
Three main findings emerged.
First, teacher-student agreement on SEI characteristics was consistently small, indicating that teachers and students often perceive classroom behavior differently.
Second, several student-rated SEI characteristics were associated with student well-being in curvilinear ways, with both too little and too much related to lower wellbeing.
Third, for a subset of SEI characteristics, teacher-student misalignment was associated with poorer well-being beyond either perspective alone.
Rank-order agreement between teacher self-ratings and class-mean student ratings averaged ρ = .17, indicating weak overall convergence.

This aligns with prior research documenting discrepancies between teacher and student perceptions across instructional behavior, emotional support, and classroom management (den Brok et al., 2006; Scherzinger & Wettstein, 2018).

text.text: Critically, these discrepancies should not be dismissed as measurement error: external observers tend to align more closely with student perceptions than with teacher self-reports (De Jong & Westerhof, 2001; Scherzinger & Wettstein, 2018), suggesting that student ratings capture meaningful classroom variation that teachers may overlook.

text.text: The pattern of agreement in our data is consistent with the interpersonal perception model (Kenny, 1994): agreement was strongest for behaviorally salient and observable items such as using personal anecdotes and following a lesson plan, whereas internal beliefs and subtle relational processes showed near-zero correlations.
Interestingly, agreement was also low for teaching pace and making learning materials creative and attractive, despite these being relatively observable behaviors.

This suggests that observability alone does not guarantee convergence when a behavior is inherently subjective -teaching pace depends partly on each perceiver's processing capacity and prior knowledge (Reilly, 1998), and judgments of creativity likely reflect different aesthetic standards between teachers and students.

text.text: These curvilinear patterns emerged across relational and social-emotional domains (trusting students, patience, emotional self-control), instructional pacing, growth mindset beliefs, and teachers' selfimprovement orientation.

Items related to connecting with students, empathic awareness, humor, behavioral management, and epistemic curiosity showed no significant associations with well-being, suggesting that optimality effects are domain-specific rather than universal.

Notably, teaching and speaking pace showed both curvilinear and negative linear components, indicating directional asymmetry: being perceived as too fast was more detrimental than being perceived as too slow.
This is consistent with cognitive load theory (Sweller, 2011) and evidence that accelerated speech degrades comprehension once input rates exceed processing limits (Peelle & Davis, 2012).

text.text: More broadly, these findings challenge the implicit "more is better" assumption in much educational research and suggest that effective teaching involves calibration rather than maximization.

Adding the teacher × student interaction term significantly improved model fit for seven SEI characteristics, indicating that perceptual alignment carries incremental associative value for student well-being beyond either perspective alone.

Across all seven effects, the curvature of the line of incongruence (a4) was consistently negative, consistent with a mismatch penalty: well-being was highest when teacher and student ratings converged and lower as discrepancies grew, regardless of direction.
One interpretation is that perceptual discrepancies undermine students' sense of being understood and effectively taught.

When teachers believe they are providing adequate support for struggling students, while students do not share this perception, students may feel invisible or misunderstood -with potential consequences for trust and engagement (Pianta et al., 2003; Quin, 2017).

text.text: Discrepancies in perceived pacing similarly suggest failures of instructional calibration.

This interpretation is consistent with research on teacher-student relationship quality showing that incongruent perceptions are associated with less positive student outcomes (Liu et al., 2023), and with evidence from organizational research that perceptual congruence between leaders and employees constitutes a resource in itself -when both parties share the same reading of a situation, interactions feel more predictable and expectations clearer (Černe et al., 2013; Gibson et al., 2009).

text.text: Although the power dynamics in classrooms differ from those in organisations, the underlying mechanism -that shared understanding reduces ambiguity and supports functioning -appears to translate across contexts.

A key strength of this study is the comprehensive assessment of teachers' SEI characteristics, spanning bonding with students, emotion regulation, behavioral management, instructional competencies, and innovative characteristics (e.g., creative teaching, openness to diversity).
This broad coverage is based on the taxonomy of Scheirlinckx and colleagues (2026) and enables a more fine-grained test of which SEI characteristic is most strongly linked to students' well-being.
By looking at a multitude of teacher characteristics, we reduce the risk that conclusions hinge on a narrow operationalization of "effective" teaching behaviors.

A second strength is the use of the TLTM response format-and the broader "calibration" perspective it embodies-which treats SEI characteristics not as simple "more is better" quantities but as behaviors that can be underused, well-calibrated, or overused depending on the classroom context and the student's needs.

This approach likely mitigates several drawbacks of traditional Likert-type ratings, including acquiescent responding and response-style artifacts (e.g., systematic avoidance of endpoints or midpoint preferences) that can distort between-person comparisons and attenuate associations with outcomes (Van Vaerenbergh & Thomas, 2013).

text.text: At the same time, complementing TLTM ratings with nonsurvey methods (e.g., systematic observations, experience sampling, or open-ended student feedback) would provide richer insight into the behavioral manifestations of SEI characteristics and could help explain why some SEI domains show robust well-being associations whereas others do not.
Several limitations warrant consideration.
First, the cross-sectional design precludes causal inference.

Although SEI characteristics are modeled as predictors, it is equally plausible that students' well-being shapes their perceptions of teacher behavior, or that unmeasured variables such as school climate influence both.

The association between misalignment and well-being is particularly susceptible to reverse causality: students with lower well-being may perceive their teachers' behavior more negatively, artificially inflating apparent discrepancies.
Longitudinal and intervention designs are needed to establish temporal precedence.
Second, the assumption that the TLTM scale midpoint represents the true optimum for all behaviors remains untested.

For some characteristics, the empirically observed optimum may deviate from the midpoint, and anchoring optimal levels against external criteria -such as observer ratings or student outcome benchmarks -would strengthen interpretability.
Third, the significant effects represent a minority of tested items, and effect sizes are modest.
While this is partly expected given the item-level analytical approach and the conservative multiple testing correction, readers should interpret the findings with this base rate in mind.
Statistically significant associations do not automatically imply practical significance, and effect sizes should be considered alongside theoretical plausibility.

Finally, despite efforts to protect anonymity (e.g., omitting personal identifiers on the paper surveys), students' responses on well-being and evaluations of their teacher may have been affected by social survey completion in the classroom, which may have introduced social desirability bias, particularly for adolescent students for whom belonging concerns are salient (King, 2024).

text.text: Future work could strengthen anonymity procedures or collect data outside class time.
These findings carry several implications for educational research and practice.
First, they reinforce calls for multi-informant assessment of teaching quality (Fauth et al., 2019; Lauermann & Hagen, 2021).
text.formatted: First, they reinforce calls for multi-informant assessment of teaching quality <ref type="bibr" target="#b10">(Fauth et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Lauermann & Hagen, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Teacher self-reports alone appear insufficient for capturing classroom-relevant SEI variation, and student perspectives offer a complementary lens on relational and emotional dynamics that students are uniquely positioned to observe.

Practically, this supports embedding structured student feedback cycles -short surveys, reflection, and goal-setting -into school-level professional development, building on evidence that student feedback can be implemented feasibly and contribute to improvements in practice (Finefter-Rosenbluh, 2021).

text.text: Second, the prevalence of curvilinear associations challenges the maximisation logic implicit in much educational intervention research.
Effective teaching appears to involve calibration and balance rather than simply doing more of what works.

Intervention designs should target optimal ranges of key behaviors rather than promoting uniformly higher levels, and help teachers recognise when initially beneficial practices begin to cross into excess (Pierce & Aguinis, 2013).
text.formatted: Intervention designs should target optimal ranges of key behaviors rather than promoting uniformly higher levels, and help teachers recognise when initially beneficial practices begin to cross into excess <ref type="bibr" target="#b31">(Pierce & Aguinis, 2013)</ref>.

text.text: Third, the mismatch penalty effect suggests that reducing perceptual gaps between teachers and students may be a low-burden avenue for supporting well-being.

Structured feedback in which teachers reflect on student perceptions -particularly in the domains where alignment was most consequential, including support for struggling students, patience, stress regulation, and pacing -could help teachers calibrate their practice to how students actually experience the classroom.

This is consistent with the prosocial classroom model (Jennings & Greenberg, 2009), which positions teachers' social-emotional awareness as foundational to building the shared understanding that supports effective classroom relationships.

text.text: This study demonstrates that teachers and students frequently perceive classroom dynamics differently, that several SEI characteristics are associated with student well-being in curvilinear ways, and that perceptual alignment between teachers and students carries incremental associative value for well-being outcomes.
These findings highlight the value of combining multiple informant perspectives and allowing for nonlinear effects when studying teaching quality.

Rather than assuming more is always better, attending to whether teacher behavior is perceived as appropriately calibrated -from the student's perspective -may better support the relational and instructional conditions associated with student well-being.
